sections.heading: Which map you see
text: Play shows the map the session has as “Map on the table”. Switch the session at the top; “All maps” opens any other map without changing what the table sees.

A map on the table is a map in play — its own copy for this session: tokens and fog live there, the map itself stays as prepared. Open a map and press Take into play (GM) to put it on the table; Start encounter does the same for an encounter and its map. Players see a map in play only after Release to players, with the fog already on.

Release also makes the map ready and open to the campaign; players get its image under the fog without sharing the image itself. A map with a cover name shows players that name until you press Reveal name under ⋯ View.
Zoom with + and −, the mouse wheel or two fingers. A sub-map that fills the view is entered; zooming out past the edge, or the arrow at the top, leads back to the map above.

On a map in play, players stay on the table map unless the GM presses Players stay here to switch it to Players change maps — then they may zoom only into maps taken into play and released in this session. The GM can always change maps.

sections.heading: Tools
text: The tool bar on the left holds the tools in groups: Select (S), Plan turn (P), Tokens (T), Measure (M), Floors (E) and Fog (F). Pick a group and its tools appear above the map; pick it again, or press Esc, to go back to Select. « hides the tool names, » shows them again.

Below a line, the same bar opens panels beside the map: Initiative (I) shows the tracker of the running encounter, Party (Y) the party and the encounters. They stay open whatever tool you use; on a phone they open above the bar.

Which groups a map shows depends on its kind, as the campaign sets it: battle maps get Walls, Fog, Light, Grid and Tokens; world, region and other maps get Sub-maps, markers and assets. GMs change it with ⚙ Tools at the end of the bar (for this kind) or under Rules & options › Map tools (all kinds).

Sub-maps › Link map: drag a frame, pick the map that lies there — zooming in then leads to it; Unlink removes it. Link shape taps the corners of a free shape instead: corners snap to walls, the grid and other shapes, Undo point or Backspace takes one back, Enter finishes. While a tool is active, frames do not lead into the sub-map.

Zooming enters a sub-map only where the cursor (mouse wheel) or the centre of the view lies; Enter when it fills shows where you are now, Use current takes it. Walls: Undo point or Backspace while drawing, Undo or Ctrl/Cmd+Z for the last change.

Sub-maps › Link settings: per linked map, how much of the view it must fill before zooming in enters it, how the GM and the players see it (click to jump, frame only, icon, hidden), and whether it shows this map faded around it. The campaign default is under Rules & options › Map.

Align to parent grid (in Link settings) sizes the sub-map from both scales and snaps it to this map's grid; both grids show while Sub-maps is open. It needs a length in both scales — not “1 day”. Measuring inside a sub-map also shows the distance in the unit of the map above; Add to route keeps legs across maps and sums them up.

Markers and tokens of a sub-map show on the map above at their place, smaller and dashed — many as one number that leads in. A marker the GM sets on the map above inside a sub-map's area shows in the sub-map under To place: Confirm puts it at the suggested spot, Move… where you tap, Keep on … leaves it on the map above.

Select: drag a marker to move it, tap it for its quick view. Measure: tap two points. Tokens (GM): Add marker — tap where it goes, then pick the article: one line per name, the creature first (then statblock, then image), + shows the others. Remove — tap a marker to take it off the map; or tap a token in Select and use Remove above it, or press Delete.
Place combatants puts the creatures of the running encounter on the map, Clear play tokens removes them again — prepared markers and the party stay.
Markers show as (Tokens, GM): Symbol (initials), Name (symbol and name), Image (token or picture) or Quick card (the article’s quick view, small). Tap a marker in Select to set it for that one alone.
Without a choice a map follows its kind (Rules & options › Marker view by map kind), then the article type (Registry › On a map), else the image.

Notes (N, GM): Add note, tap the map, write the text and choose GM only or Players too. A note is its own article; it stands as a small card and moves like any marker. Players never get a GM note, not even its marker.
Fullscreen (or Shift+F) gives the map the whole screen; Esc leaves it.

Floors (E): a map with several floors — storeys, a cellar, tower levels — shows the floor you see in the bar; pick Floors to switch between them. Stairs, ladders, bridges and portals are the square markers, some with a dashed area: tap one to see where it leads, Show the other floor, or take a token standing in its area through. A token on stairs you can see through sees both floors.

A token dropped on a portal goes through at once. The GM can Send all through, also through a portal to another map — the session follows. In an encounter, take a passage in Plan turn: it costs what the campaign or the passage says. GMs add floors and passages under Floors.

Party (Y) shows the party beside the map: hit points and conditions, ◎ centres the map on a token. The GM places a character with Place or by dragging its row onto the map, and sees the encounters of the session with Place for the combatants not yet on the map.

Before an encounter starts, Prepare sets its combatants on the map faded and hidden from the players; drag them where they belong. ▶ Start rolls initiative for whoever has none (into the log), reveals the prepared tokens and makes the encounter the one the session runs.

View as (GM) shows the map as the GM, as all players or as one character: fogged parts covered, hidden markers left out. On a phone the tools stay below the map at the bottom of the screen, and View as and release sit behind ⋯ View.

sections.heading: Initiative tracker
text: Initiative in the tool bar opens the tracker of the encounter the session runs beside the map — on a computer it starts open, on a phone closed. Without a map it stands on the page. It lists the combatants by initiative, marks whose turn it is and shows the round; ⛶ shows it full screen for a projector.

GM: ▶ Start rolls initiative and runs the encounter; Next turn ends the current turn, counts effects down and starts the next; ◀ goes back without bringing expired effects back. Tap an initiative to change it.

Skip passes over the current combatant, ⤒ goes back to the top in the same round, and ▸ on a row makes that combatant current — none of these count effects down. The head shows the round and, for the GM, Turn x/y.

Each row has the quick actions the campaign picked — Damage, Heal, Effect, Reroll, Remove — and 👁 shows or hides a foe from the players. Combatants without recorded hit points are at full. Add a combatant at the bottom.
Damage asks for its type (fire, slashing …): the server takes off what is left after resistances, immunities and vulnerabilities, temporary hit points first, and the line above the order says why.

A combatant who concentrates makes the Constitution save at once (DC 10 or half the damage), rolled into the log. A player character's hit points stay the same in the tracker and on the character sheet.

▾ opens a row with what the combatant can do: traits, actions, bonus actions, reactions and spells from its statblock, with rolls. Players see this for the party, and for foes only if the campaign shows foes' actions.
When a turn changes, the new row lights up briefly; ✦ turns this off for your account, and it stays still if your device asks for reduced motion.

An effect is a condition or a note with a duration: it counts down at the start or end of a combatant's turn — its own or another's — and drops at zero. Without rounds it stays until removed; hidden effects show only to the GM.

Players see the party, and a foe once its turn has come; what else they see — cover names, health as nothing, a word or numbers, effects, actions — is the campaign's choice under Rules & options › Combat.
When it is your turn, End turn passes it on. Rules & options › Combat › Initiative picks the initiative system — D&D 5e (standard) — or turns the tracker off.

sections.heading: Moving your token
text: Outside an encounter, drag your own character's token. Depending on the campaign it moves at once, or it leaves a dashed proposal that the GM confirms (✓) or rejects (✗); everyone who sees the token sees the proposal. During an encounter, your token moves through the turn plan.

Which tokens you may drag is the campaign's choice (Rules & options › Who moves tokens): none, your own characters, the whole party, the party and its allies in an encounter, or every token. GMs: Tokens › “Movement: own · confirm” shows the setting and changes it right on the map.

sections.heading: Fog of war
text: Fog is revealed by the GM, not by creatures. You do not need to place a creature: pick Fog in the tool bar, switch “Fog on”, then reveal by hand — Reveal drags a rectangle, Brush paints (choose the width), Hide covers an area again, Reveal all and Cover all do the whole map.
“Reveal along moves” says whether moving a token on a fogged map reveals the way it went: the campaign sets the default under Rules & options › On the map, and each map may say on or off.
If the campaign keeps fog per character, choose the character under “View as”: you see what it sees, and what you reveal is for it. As GM or all players, what you reveal is for everyone.

sections.heading: Walls and doors
text: Walls (W): pick a kind and a shape — polyline (Closed joins the end to the start), line, rectangle, ellipse or polygon — then Draw: tap point after point, Enter or the last point again finishes. Set kind, Lock and Erase act on the wall you tap. Walls and closed doors block movement and sight; windows and obstacles block movement only. Players see only doors; a closed secret door is a wall to them.

A door is drawn as a line across the opening and becomes a box of the thickness you set; that box is what you click. With “Cut walls” on, a door or window drawn over a wall splits it at its edges; erasing the door offers to join the wall again.

Snap pulls a point to an existing point, a grid corner or a wall line within the strength set (screen pixels); Alt places it freely. Show points marks every corner; Points lets you drag one, and the walls meeting there move with it.
Hold on the map in Draw, Points, Set origin, Pick a square or Add marker and a loupe opens above your finger: drag to aim the crosshair, let go to place the point there.
Tap a door in Select to open or close it. Players open a door next to their token if the campaign allows (Rules & options › Doors); locked doors stay shut.

sections.heading: Setting the grid
text: Grid (G): choose square or hex, then set it on the image — Set origin taps a point where two lines cross, Pick a square taps two opposite corners of one square and takes its size. The grid shows at once; Save grid stores it, Discard goes back.

Fine-tune with the arrows (Shift: ten times as far) and the size slider, which moves within ±10 % of the size; type a number for big jumps. Show grid, Colour and Opacity change how it looks — hidden, it still measures and snaps.

Scale: 1 square (or 1 hex) = 5 ft, 10 ft, 1,5 m, 1 mi or 6 mi from the list, or type your own. Movement, reach, light and measuring use it; on a floor it applies to that floor. The bar under the map shows it.
Tokens snap to the grid (on by default): a dropped token lands so that it covers whole squares — large creatures 2×2, huge 3×3.

Tokens › Token size gives a token its own size — how many squares it covers, half squares included; “by size” follows its statblock and effects such as Enlarge or Reduce, and a dashed square with a label shows the choice and where the size comes from. Rules & options › Token sizes says whether a tiny creature takes half a square.

When several size effects overlap (Enlarged and Reduced), they do not add up: the latest applies and the token says “2 size effects — choose”; tap the token and pick under “Size effect that applies” which one counts. When an effect's duration runs out in the initiative, the size falls back.

sections.heading: Line of sight
text: With walls on a map, moves (if they reveal) and opened doors uncover what the characters see, up to the next wall. Without walls a move reveals a strip two squares wide; without a moving token, the GM reveals by hand.

sections.heading: Assets on the map
text: On the map's own page (editing), Tokens › Add asset places a crate, a table or a lantern; Tokens › Asset sets the one you tap: size in squares, height ÷ width, rotation, Movable in play, and Blocks — like a wall, a window, an obstacle or an invisible wall. Drag any asset there to move it.

Assets are fixed by default. In Play, only an asset marked Movable in play can be dragged — always by the GM, and by players when the campaign lets them move more than their own character and moves need no confirmation. It moves on the map in play, not on the original. Give an asset light with Light › Light source.

sections.heading: Light and darkvision
text: Light › Lighting sets the map bright, dim or dark. Light source: set bright and dim light in squares, then tap the map to place a light there, or a token, asset or marker to make it shine — blocked by walls but not by windows. 0 and 0 takes the light away. While Light is open, circles show how far each light reaches; on a bright map lights change nothing until Lighting is dim or dark.

In the dark, a character sees only what its darkvision reaches (from Senses on its statblock) and the lights it can see; moves and opened doors reveal just that. Players see darkness over the map with lights and their darkvision cut out.

On a fogged map, players see brightly what their character sees right now, and what was revealed before dimmed. Sight comes from the player characters' tokens; the party token counts only while none of them is on the map.

With walls, players see only up to the next wall or closed door, fog or not. In the dark, what only darkvision reaches is shown in greyscale; lit areas keep their colour. An item with Bright light (a torch, a lantern) lights the token of the character holding it in hand, and lights itself when placed as a marker. Light on/off switches a light off and on again without losing its radius.

On a dark map, players get only the tokens their characters see — with darkvision or in a light they can see into. A creature waiting in the dark is not on their map at all until a light or a character's darkvision reaches it.

sections.heading: Draw on the map
text: Draw (D) puts strokes on a drawing layer of their own: Pen, Line, Rectangle or Ellipse, in a colour and width. Without a layer chosen, the first stroke makes one. Erase takes away the stroke you tap. GM only keeps the chosen layer from the players; Layers above the map shows and hides drawing layers like image layers.
Text places a label you type, Stamp a symbol (danger, warning, flag …), both where you tap and in the size you choose; Erase takes them away like strokes.

sections.heading: Lock the map level
text: The lock next to Fit keeps zooming on this map: + and −, the wheel and two fingers only zoom, no sub-map is entered and zooming out does not lead to the map above. Breadcrumbs and clicking a frame still go there. The lock stays for this browser.

sections.heading: Zones and territories
text: A zone (a rule such as difficult terrain or magical darkness, an article of the kind Zone kind) and a territory (who holds the ground: a faction, a realm) lie on the map as coloured squares — every square whose centre lies in the shape. Without a grid the shape itself is drawn. Each belongs to one floor.

Areas above the map hides and shows them, just for you. Players see only areas on articles they may see, and on a fogged map only what is revealed; a zone whose kind is hidden until noticed stays with the GM, dashed, until its link is marked Found — then players see it at once.

To draw one, open Zones (Z) in the tool bar, pick a zone kind or a faction under For, then drag a Rectangle or Ellipse or tap the corners of a Polygon. Found, then tapping a hidden zone, shows it to players at that spot; Remove takes an area away — the zone kind or faction stays.

sections.heading: Turn planner and reactions
text: During an encounter, players plan their turn with the tool Plan turn (P) in the tool bar: pick actions, tap squares to move, then “Send turn to GM”. Player tokens move only through the plan. Plan turn appears only for your own characters — a player without one does not see it; the GM plans for every creature and sees a number for turns waiting.
How much a player plans is the campaign's choice (Rules & options › Combat › Turn planner): off, movement only, movement and actions, or full with reactions.
A square marked ⚠ leaves an enemy's reach and provokes an opportunity attack — Disengage first to avoid it. The GM confirms a plan with “Confirm & roll” or sends it back.

Confirming rolls at the server and applies the result: damage comes off the target's hit points after its resistances, immunities and vulnerabilities, and a target that concentrates makes its Constitution save against the DC at once.
Dodge, Help, Hide and Ready leave an entry in the initiative that counts down: attacks against a dodging creature have disadvantage, a helped or hidden one attacks with advantage once.

Moving, the path may pass through allies but not stop on them, and difficult terrain (a zone on the map whose zone kind has Movement cost × 2) costs double — such squares show brown. The server counts the feet again when the turn is sent, so a path that is too long is refused.

The hit chance on each target already counts advantage and disadvantage from conditions (“adv.”, “dis.”). A target beyond an attack's range cannot be picked: the line under the turn says why, and the server refuses such a turn too; between normal and long range the attack rolls with disadvantage, and the step says “long range”.
Range counts from where your planned move ends to the nearest square the target takes up — a huge dragon you touch is 5 ft away.
As the turn plays out, whoever may react is asked “Opportunity attack?”. Attack rolls into the log and uses the reaction until that creature's next turn.

With Rules from graphs on (Rules & options › At the table), the rule articles in play decide instead: a rule may offer a reaction when someone leaves a reach, is attacked, hit, missed or damaged — Shield, Sentinel, an opportunity attack. Use takes it and spends the reaction, Skip lets it pass; other outcomes appear as a line in the turn’s result for the GM to apply.
Every map you can see, with a preview; sub-maps stand indented under their map. Filter by layer and tag.

Transformations › + Group by … groups the maps by map kind, location (the place the map shows, or the place of its parent map), region (the outermost place above it), layer, parent map or tag, with a count per group; ▾ closes a group. Your grouping is kept for your account; Save… names it, Copy link shares it. Without a step the list stays the tree by parent map.
“New map” turns an uploaded or chosen image into a map. To put a map on the table, set “Map on the table” on the session — then it shows under Play.
All images you can see. Filter by kind, tag, layer, or “unused” for images nothing refers to yet.
Each image names its resolution, aspect ratio, size and layer. Tags stand as badges: × removes one, “+ tag” adds one; select several images to tag them together.
“Use as…” turns an image into a map (with a grid suggested from its resolution), a creature's token or a prop, and links to the result.

Delete removes the selected images — or one image with 🗑 — but only those in your write layer; images from other layers are deselected, and the message says how many. Undo right after brings them back, and for 30 days they wait in Deleted; to delete the others, switch your write layer in the header.

Upload images opens your device's file menu: on a phone Files, OneDrive and other storage as well as photos and the camera. Any file can be chosen; it is checked afterwards — JPEG, PNG, WebP, GIF and AVIF go up, anything else (HEIC, SVG, PDF …) says what to do instead. Animated GIF and WebP are kept as they are.

The assistant walks through a character step by step: ancestry, class, background, ability scores, each open choice, then the name. A step you are unsure of can be left with “Decide later”. Its steps and options come from the articles in play — what the campaign's layers bring. A long step (a class with its choices, the equipment) has ‹ and › to go from one choice to the next (Alt+↑/↓).
An Ability Score Improvement asks again at each level that grants it: +2 to one score, +1 to two, or a feat where the campaign allows feats.

Started under New article? “Use the character builder” there takes along what you entered — the name, the layer and required fields — so the assistant does not ask again. A character created there first opens in the assistant with what it already has: class, ancestry and scores count as earlier choices.

“Edit” on a character opens the same assistant with every step. To level up, raise a class in the class step with + — or add another class (multiclass), which by the rules needs the minimum scores of every class you have and of the new one. What the new level asks for, and its hit points, follow as steps “Full edit” on the article is the plain field form.

A spellcaster chooses its cantrips and spells as steps — from the spell list of its class, up to the highest level it casts; level up adds the new ones. A spell you already have from another source is locked.

What an earlier step already gives — a skill, tool or language from your ancestry, background or class, or a feat that cannot be taken twice — is locked in later choices and says where it comes from. Change an earlier choice and a later one that now doubles it is marked, not cleared: pick another. If a source gives something you already chose, the rules let you choose another one instead.

Expertise only goes on a skill or tool the character is already proficient in — from a fixed source or an earlier choice, including one made just before in the same step. The others are locked and say “not proficient yet”. A choice whose data says it needs no proficiency (Needs proficiency switched off) offers everything.
Under the title stands the layer: of the character when you edit it or level it up, and the layer a new character goes into — change that under “Writes to” in the header.

An article as a page of a book. “Edit” changes it; on an article you cannot write, Edit makes your own version in a layer of yours. Click a named article for its quick view; “Open article” goes there.

The page has chapters: Fields (the article itself), Relations, Linked here, Admin and Log. On a phone they are tabs at the top; the chosen one stays in the address (?k=admin), so Back and a shared link keep it. A chapter with nothing in it does not show.

On a wider screen the chapters are framed areas: the fields on the left, relations and what links here on the right, Admin and Log below, collapsed until you open them. The row above them jumps to each.

Expand all and Collapse all open and close Admin and Log (and the groups inside, such as a layer’s contents by type); ‹ and › go from section to section (Alt+↑/↓, with Shift: collapse/expand all). Whether Admin and Log stand open is kept for your account.
Fields that suggest (an encounter’s kind, a place type) offer their list and the values already in use as you type — pick one or type your own. A colour field opens a colour picker.

Edit starts with the Layer field: the layer this article belongs to. Choose another layer you write in (the same list as Writes to in the header, also layers this campaign does not turn on, marked “not in this campaign”) and Save moves it there; the page then says where it is now. Its links, versions and parts stay where they are. Only the administration can take an article out of every layer.

Under the title stands only the layer of this version. Admin, on every kind of article, names all its layers and those of its other versions — click one to open that version — and why you see it: in play, from a compare layer, enabled as extra content, or in no layer.
Admin also says who can see it, with the level that applies and where it comes from (set here, a campaign rule, the layer’s default), what is known about it, its versions and its source.

Text sections — read-aloud text, notes, secrets — are long text of a kind the type offers; they are not rows in the field list, because each section can be revealed on its own. The Fields chapter lists the kinds with how many stand here; “+ Text” adds one, also in Edit.
“Print” puts the article on an A4 sheet. Versions of the same article in other layers can be compared side by side.
A creature without an image of its own shows the image of its statblock, or its token. Give it an image and that one shows instead.

On a character, “How the numbers come about” shows each number with where it comes from: the armor and shield worn, items, features, conditions, the statblock. Resistances, immunities and a lowered critical-hit threshold show there too. The initiative tracker and the turn plan read the same numbers.

Above a statblock’s legendary actions stands how many it can take each round; when it has more in its lair (the field “Legendary actions in lair”), the sentence says so: “3 legendary actions (4 in its lair)”.

The token of a statblock — on a creature, of its statblock — stands as it does on the map. “Adjust token” drags and zooms the image in its circle, picks its border, or marks it as a ready-made round token that is shown as it is; frame and border are saved on the image, so every statblock with that token looks the same. “Change image” sets another image as the token of the statblock.

GMs see a Knowledge box at the side: which pieces of information exist about this article — on it, for it, or for a whole group — the fields each covers and the knowledge it belongs to. “+ Information” picks fields by group and ticks or names a knowledge; who knows it is set on the knowledge.

A knowledge’s page writes out everything it brings together: each information with the articles it is about and exactly the fields it covers — read as you may read them. Players find what their character knows in one place.

Delete removes the article if it lies in your write layer and you may write it; otherwise the message names the layer to switch to. Undo right after the deletion brings it back with its links; for 30 days it can also be restored from Deleted.

sections.heading: Layers: reading a book
text: A layer's page shows its book below the header, chapter after chapter. The table of contents opens at the side; its chapters fold out.
Search finds a passage in this book. Where you stopped is remembered for your account, on every device. A group of layers shows as a shelf.
‹ and › above the text go to the previous or next section, and on to the next chapter at the end (Alt+↑ and Alt+↓). On a phone they sit at the bottom of the screen.
Pictures stand where the book has them, with their caption. Until the picture itself is uploaded, a frame with the caption holds its place.

sections.heading: Layers: what a source brings
text: Contents lists the articles of a layer by type, each linked; a group lists its layers. The ticks show what the current campaign has in play.

The GM turns the layer on or off, picks which types it brings, and enables single articles from a source that is not in play. Articles that come with the layer stay ticked; a layer brought by its group or a type rule is chosen on the campaign page.

sections.heading: Classes, ancestries and backgrounds
text: A class shows its level table, its subclasses to pick and compare, and its features by level; an ancestry or background its variants and traits.

sections.heading: Characters: the sheet
text: A character's page has its header above the tabs: hit points with an amount — type it, use − and + or scroll over it — for Damage, Heal and Temp. Damage takes temporary hit points first; temporary hit points don't stack, the higher value stays. The arrows switch between vitals and spellcasting; hit dice, spell slots and inspiration are pips you click.

Rest: “Short · hit die” rolls one hit die into the log and heals the roll plus your CON modifier; “Long rest” (asked once more) brings back all hit points, half your hit dice, every spell slot, and takes one level of exhaustion away. What it changed shows below.

The status row below shows concentration, conditions with how long they last and whether you are hidden; × removes one, “+ Condition” adds one. Damage while concentrating asks for the Constitution save (DC 10 or half the damage); “Failed” ends the spell. “▴ Less” collapses the header to hit points, damage and heal, AC, initiative and speed; on a phone it starts collapsed.
Overview, Combat, Gear, Crafting and Ties are tabs; a link such as the gold in the header opens its tab.

Gear starts with your hands. Tap an item — in the grid, in the list or under “Not stowed” — then tap Main hand or Off hand; with a mouse you can also drag it there. A two-handed weapon takes both hands, a shield only the off hand; One hand / Two hands switches the grip of a versatile weapon.
If a hand is full, a warning asks whether to stow what is there, drop it (free) or cancel. Stow puts a held item back into the grid, or under “Not stowed” when there is no room.

Beside the hands, the picked item lists every place it can go: ✓ fits, ⚠ moves something else out, ✗ not there, with the reason. Under the hands, ✓ and ✗ say what your hands allow right now — spellcasting, a shield without training, a free hand for a potion — and Your turn in Combat locks the same actions with the same reason.

Log, at the bottom, lists the rolls made on the character and on its statblock, newest first; filter by who rolled or by session. On the statblock, click a skill or saving throw bonus (Stealth +6, Dex +4) or an ability modifier to roll it — Shift for advantage, Alt for disadvantage; the log says what was rolled.

Below the statblock on Overview, “Proficiencies and where they come from” lists saving throws, proficiencies and expertise, each with its source — class, background, origin, feature, feat, a choice you made, an item, or added by hand on the statblock — linked to that article. Crafting, the sheet and “usable by” count exactly these.

Below that, “How the numbers come about” opens each value — abilities as base plus origin, background, choices and items; proficiency bonus, hit points, AC, initiative, speed, senses — each part linked to its article.
Header, statblock and quick view show these final numbers. The statblock keeps the base scores, and editing writes there.

Combat starts with Your turn: every action by type (Action, Bonus, Reaction, Free, Trigger). The chips filter by type; Sources picks which features, spells and items show. Click Action, Bonus or Reaction under Used once spent; New turn clears them.
A blocked action stays with 🔒 and the reason — a spell without a free hand, for instance. Click a row for its toolbar: use it, open its article, see details, undo.

Spells shows ability, spell attack, save DC, slots and concentration on top, then every spell by level. Cast uses the lowest free slot of its level or higher, starts concentration for a concentration spell and marks the action used; a ritual needs no slot. Blocked shows why. Below: your class spell lists, what is possible for you now, and how you learn spells — other ways fold out.

Your classes give the spellcasting ability and the slots for your level; your origin, feats, features and the items you hold add their spells, and the spells you chose in the character assistant stand there too. A value set on the statblock by hand wins.
Each spell names its source. One cast with another ability than the header — a cantrip of your origin, say — shows that ability with its save DC and attack.

Crafting lists your blueprints: what you know or all of them, ready now, almost, by tool. Pick one for its workbench — materials from you and your party, then Start crafting. Your running orders stand below with their checks as circles.

Campaign shows what the campaign gave your character: handouts (letters, maps, pictures and knowledge you hold), sessions, quests, people, encounters, maps and places. It only holds what the server lets you see.

sections.heading: Sessions
text: A session article holds what is happening at the table: the map on the table, the running encounter and the scene. What the GM sets here reaches every screen at once — Play follows it.

sections.heading: Encounters
text: An encounter shows what its kind needs: a conversation (social) lists who takes part — the creatures and factions it features — with what each thinks of the party; change that on the creature, under its relationships. A trap or hazard shows its hazards as cards.
GM: under each hint of a puzzle, “Reveal to the party” tells the party that one hint and nothing else; a revealed hint says “The party knows this hint”.

sections.heading: Crafting (recipes)
text: On a recipe, “Start crafting” makes a crafting order. Its material stays reserved in the inventory of the character and the party until the order ends.

“Work a day” advances an order. Where the recipe asks for a check, “Roll check” rolls a d20 plus the crafter's bonus from their statblock (ability, tool proficiency) on the server, into the order's log; or enter a total you rolled at the table. The GM accepts or rejects the result. How long crafting takes and what it costs are the campaign's rules.

sections.heading: Inventory
text: Characters, parties and containers carry items in a grid: drag to move, rotate a piece, move it between character, party and container. Zones of a container say how long it takes to draw what lies there.
A piece whose shape is not symmetric can also be mirrored. Its picture lies in its cells, turned and mirrored with it.

Tap a piece on the cell you want to hold it by — that cell is marked — then tap a free cell: the piece lands with that cell there. Tap another of its cells to hold it there instead. A piece from Not stowed is held by the first cell of its top row.

Discard takes a piece out of the game: say how many of a stack, confirm, and the piece is deleted with the last one. Undo right after puts it back where it was — as long as nothing else changed in that inventory.

Sell offers the shops you can see with what each pays for one piece; the shops where the scene or map in play is come first, under Here. Pick a shop and a quantity: the coins go into the purse of the inventory you sell from. From the party’s chest, every member sells for the party.
A piece reserved for a crafting order can’t be discarded or sold — the message says so; release it first.

sections.heading: Item shape
text: On an item, Shape shows the cells it takes in the grid inventory, with its picture, as Grid or List; Rotate and Mirror there are only a preview.

Edit shape paints the cells on a 5 × 5 grid that grows when you paint its last row or column, or takes the rows as text (# taken, . free; X and 0 work too), with the stack size. Empty borders are cut off when you save.
Adjust inventory image picks an own picture or keeps the item’s image, and sets fit or fill, zoom, a quarter turn and the part that shows by dragging.

sections.heading: Enhancements and item properties
text: +1 Weapon, Silvered or Adamantine Armor are enhancements: rules articles of their own (Rules › Enhancement), not items. On a piece in an inventory, add one under Enhancements; the piece’s name, price, rarity and bonuses are worked out from the base item and what is on it.

Item properties such as Finesse or Versatile are rules articles too. What one does on the sheet is its field “On the sheet” (two-handed, versatile, light, finesse), not its name — a house property can take both hands under any name. What it means for one item, such as Versatile 1d10 or Thrown 20/60, stands on that item’s edge “has property”.

sections.title: Views of an article
text: A row “View” above every article — on its page and when opened from World, Story, Rules or Play — lists every view that applies to it, the most specific first. Full is the page as always; pick another to see the article in it. The choice stays in the address (?view=) and is not saved; in Full edit the row stands for whoever may change the registry.

“Design this view” opens the view designer beside the article — on a phone as a sheet from below — and the page above shows the draft. Pick another view to start from under Design. Save for every article, for every article of this type (preselected), for this article only, or as a new view with a condition.
One view of the article on an A4 sheet. Choose the view, then print with your browser (Ctrl+P).
The article on the left, another version of it on the right, field by field. “Only differences” hides what is the same.

World, Story and Rules are areas; the Compendium holds everything. Narrow the list in the sidebar by type, tag and status; the columns come from each type's overview — a place shows its type and environment, a quest its progress and reward, a faction its kind.
Above the filters, Expand all and Collapse all open and close every filter; ‹ and › go from one to the next. Which filters stand open is kept for your account, for each page and type.
“Columns” picks what the table shows: any field of the type (also calculated ones), its edges, and what every row has — type, source, layers, tags, status, ID. Drag or use ↑↓ to order them.

The choice is kept per page and type for your account and in the address, so a shared link shows the same table. “Reset to default” drops your choice: the campaign default shows, else the type's columns. The GM can make a choice the campaign default for everyone without their own.

Filter groups are saved filters of a page — reach them as tabs or from ▾ in the header. The layers shown follow the running campaign; change them in the popup under the brand. There, “Show comparison articles in lists” adds what only a comparison layer brings, below the list and marked “not in play”; the GM brings one into play with “Enable”.

Pick one type and its fields become filters. Where a type has a prerequisite (feats, magic items, classes), “Usable by” keeps what a character meets; a “?” marks a prerequisite that could not be checked.

When & who filters by when an article was added or last changed — today, the last 7 or 30 days, or between two dates — and by who added it; Sort puts the newest first. The choice stays in the address and in a saved filter group, and holds when you change the type.

Relations filters by an article's links and fields: has a link (member of, carries …), has none, at least or at most so many, or linked to one article you pick; with a type chosen also has a field, such as an item's Shape. Several conditions all apply. Only what you may see counts.
“New article” creates one in your write layer.

A Collection under Rules groups articles — Simple Melee Weapons, Damage Types. Its members come by rule (types, tags, field conditions) and by hand: link an article with “in collection”, or tick Exclude to take one out. Its page lists the members.
A board is a canvas for one story article: place articles on it as cards, arrange them, and choose how large each card shows.

sections.title: Tools
text: The tool bar stands on the left (on a phone at the bottom): Select, Article, Query, Structure, Text, Image, Draw, Map, Background and Area. The chosen tool shows its options above the canvas; Esc goes back to Select.

Text: choose a heading, paragraph, list or quote, then click the canvas. A note longer than its box scrolls inside it; drag its corner to make it larger. It is Markdown — [[links]] and {VAR} work as everywhere and are filled in when shown, never in what is saved. Image: upload one or choose from the images. Draw: freehand, line, arrow, rectangle or ellipse, with colour and width.

Select an element to change it in the panel over the canvas — text, colour, fill, width, turn, front or back, GM only — or press Delete. GM only on an element or on a card (the GM button) keeps it from players altogether.

Map: a map as a live card, or as the background — it fills the canvas under the cards; players see only what they would see in play. Background: an image (stretched, tiled or once), a colour, or a map.

sections.title: Query cards
text: Query (⚄ in the tool bar) places a card that shows a selection instead of one article. ⚙ on the card sets its source — types, tags, layers, single articles and a filter chain such as filter:status=ready — and how it shows: a list, Draw or a slideshow.

Draw takes one at random and does not put it back until Reset; everyone at the table sees the same draws. With Reveal when drawn, what is drawn becomes knowledge of the party and visible to it. A slideshow turns on by itself; ‹ › step, ⛶ shows it full screen for a second screen.
Players see only the articles they may see — the card asks the server for each of them.

Live from the campaign: a card can ask for the scene in play, the current arc, the running or next session, the party or the open quests instead of naming articles. It follows the game — set another scene on the session and the card shows it.

sections.title: Structure cards
text: Structure (⌥ in the tool bar) places a card that draws a faction, place or family from its edges: ⚙ chooses the start, which edges (members and ranks, parts and sub-factions, what it controls, residents, relationships), how deep, and tree or web.

Tree is an organisation chart: ▾ folds a branch, the line from above carries the rank or the tags of the relationship, ↑ marks what the start belongs to, → and ↩ list relationships across the tree; a long tree scrolls inside the card. Web draws rings around the start and fits the whole web into the card — resize the card (corner) to see it larger; a dashed line runs across the tree.
Click a name for its quick card; + on a node shows what lies beyond the depth. Each direction of a relationship is its own line with its own tags.
Players see only the entries and lines they may see — the card asks the server for each viewer, and what hangs only on something hidden stays hidden too.

sections.title: The campaign board
text: Every campaign has a board of its own, where players land after signing in: the campaign, Now playing, Next session, The party, Open quests and Rumours. Change it like any board. Players get a bar back to it, to their character, maps, search and knowledge.

sections.title: An endless canvas
text: The canvas grows with what lies on it: drag a card or draw past the edge and there is more room. Drag the empty canvas to pan, Ctrl or ⌘ with the wheel zooms, and Fit all brings everything into view.

sections.title: Views on a card
text: A card’s view menu offers the designed views that apply to its article — for example “Shop” on a creature that keeps a shop — and after them the usual ones, Full included: the whole article page, scrolling inside the card. A card on Quick shows the most specific quick view that applies, as the popup does.
Players see a card without a chosen view as the Handout; what the GM chooses for a card counts for everyone. A map on a card is the live map itself.
The classes, ancestries and backgrounds in play. Each opens on its article page with what it grants at which level.
For the GM and administrators: checks that find articles with gaps or broken links, and bulk changes with a preview and undo.

Add edge takes an article as target, or a path over edges: <-describedIn is whatever points here with described in, ->mapOf->happensAt follows map of and then happens at. Every selected article gets its own target; one with several is skipped, not guessed.
The types of articles, their fields, edges, lists and views. A new type is a new row — create it here. Before something is removed, the registry counts what uses it.

A type’s page has chapters — This type, Own fields, Inherited, Edges from here and Views. On a phone they are tabs; on a wider screen the fields stand on the left, the short settings and the edges on the right.

Expand all opens every inherited type and Edges from here; Collapse all closes them; ‹ and › go from section to section (Alt+↑/↓). On a phone the bar sits at the bottom and works in the chosen tab. Which groups stand open is kept for your account.
“How it works” explains the model with a worked example.
Every article lies in a layer and has a state. One that fits no other layer waits in Unassigned — an ordinary layer you can switch on in a campaign; the workbench lists its articles under Unassigned.

Two views are forms for creating: Create (what the quick dialog asks when you create from a picker) and Create (full) (the article page right after New article, with its fields first, even empty). Design them per type under Views; without a design, creating works as before.
Put the element Steps in a create view to guide through pages with Back and Next. The element Character builder makes New article open the builder, as the player character does.

A field or an edge kind can be required always, or only for a state: “to be prepared” or “to be ready”. An idea may go without it, but the article can only be set to that state once it is filled; the workbench lists articles at a state that miss something under Ready with gaps. A character with an open choice stays an idea the same way.

sections.title: View designer
text: Registry › Views lists every view with its group, what it applies to and how many articles get it; “Design” opens it in the view designer — the one editor for views. The preview stands on top.

Below it the designer bar: insert by group (Fields, Links, Text, Image, Layout, Table, Graph, Game, Pages), find an element, and undo, redo, copy and paste. Then the structure as an indented tree and, on the right, the configuration and values of the selected element.

Under each view stand the types that say their own for it and the designed views of its group; the row of views at the top and “In this view” in the designer switch between them. Find an element with the search in the bar.
A selected element has its own bar at the bottom: up, down, into, out, duplicate, copy, remove, undo, done. Keys: Ctrl+Z, Ctrl+Shift+Z, Ctrl+C, Ctrl+V, Ctrl+D, Delete, Esc.

Move elements with ↑ ↓, → into the container above (a section, columns, a tab …) and ← out again, or drag them. Collapse a container to keep the tree short. Values can come from linked articles, by following an edge; “Leave out” and “Only when” say what an element skips and where it shows.

“Save for …” says where the change goes: every article (the view itself, with its name, order, the rest at the end and empty fields), every article of a type (preselected when you come from one; an adjustment where possible, else its own arrangement), one article, or a new view with a condition. Overview, Quick, Full and Print can be rebuilt but not deleted; the + of a search hit shows Quick.
A type’s page lists the views that apply to it, and from where; “Design” opens the designer with the type chosen.

Design under a selected element gives its head, surface, frame and text a token — a colour with a light and a dark value. “Use for every … in this view” makes it the view’s design for that kind of element.

sections.title: Tokens
text: Registry › Tokens lists the colours elements can use: role, light and dark value, the surface a text stands on, the contrast in both modes and how many views use each.
Add a token by name; delete one only when no view uses it. The workbench lists tokens whose contrast falls short.
One article or a condition can also be saved as an overlay: tick “as an overlay” and only what you added, moved or took away is kept, with a priority; the rest keeps following the view.

Elements from other overlays carry their name in the tree; ⚠ marks where two overlays change the same element or share a position. Overlays stand under their view in Registry › Views; the workbench lists their conflicts.

In the Layers tab every part is a section that folds: Order in play, Saved selections, each group of books, Compare layers and Extra content, each with its count in the header. Expand all and Collapse all fold them all; ‹ and › jump to the previous or next one (Alt+↑/↓, with Shift: collapse/expand all). What is folded is kept for your account.

The campaign page has tabs: Overview (the decisions and the story of the campaign), Members (who sits at the table, roles, invitations), Layers (what is switched on and in which order), Rules & options and Visibility. The tab stands in the address, so a link opens it. GMs change the members; co-GMs see them.

Decisions on the Overview lists everything the campaign has decided, one row each: layers in play, compare layers, members and roles, and every rule. Change opens the tab where just that decision is made again — for a rule, at its system. Installation settings show where they stand; the admin changes them.

Each decision says whether it is decided, a default or still open, and what a change does: ability score methods and starting equipment apply to characters made from now on, while most rules are read at once and nothing stored is rewritten.
Characters are given per campaign: a character given under Members is that member’s only in this campaign.

The page opens on the running campaign — the one in the header — and follows when it is switched there. If you pick another campaign here, the Overview says it is not the running one; the admin can make it running with “Make this the running campaign”. A new campaign can be picked in the header at once.

Rules & options shows the campaign’s choices by system. Every system, rule and option is a rule article — its name opens it. Whoever may change the campaign picks “Use this” beside an option to switch it right there. GMs see how many rules of the app still lack an article; those are not listed.
Where several may be allowed — ability score methods, starting equipment, substitutions — each has a tick: tick or untick it right there. With none ticked, the defaults apply.

Under Inventory, GMs set up Basil’s sheet as blocks: each block is a grid with its own zones — select cells, make a zone, give it a duration — and conditions such as a size or a strength. Every block that applies is joined into one grid; “Try it” shows the result for a size and a STR score. Container templates get zones the same way.

“View as” on a member — or “View as ▾” under the campaign in the header, on every page (Alt+Shift+V) — shows the site as that member sees it, read only. The band at the top says whose view it is; “Exit” or Alt+Shift+V goes back.

“Order in play” lists every layer and group in play, top first: the higher one counts where two bring a version of the same article. Drag a row by its handle (or use ↑ ↓); a group moves as a block. Drag a book out of its group, or use “Own place”, to give it its own place; “Back into …” returns it.
Each row says what its place does: which articles it replaces, and where its versions lose.

Visibility shows who sees what, per group: rows are groups (layer, then type — change the steps above the table), columns are Public, Table, each player and GM, each cell how many articles of the group that column sees.

Pick an audience for a group, click a player's cell to show or hide the group for that player only, ↺ goes back to the layer's default. Articles with their own setting win over the group; “own” lists them, and “Follow the group” removes their setting.

Below the groups, under Layers and under Visibility, “Articles and their layers” lists every article in play with its layer, the layer's publisher, its visibility and where that comes from (own setting, campaign rule, layer default). Filter by name, layer, type and visibility, sort by name, layer, type or visibility.

An article in a layer you do not write — a rulebook several campaigns share — can be set here too: what you choose becomes a rule of this campaign for that one article (“campaign (this article)”), and the book stays as it is. Such a rule wins over every group; the article’s own setting still wins over it. ↺ removes it.

An article with more than one version says so in its row: which one lists and links show, and Prefer this version for the others. Under Layers › Order in play, First for some types puts one layer first for a type only.

To move articles to another layer, tick them, choose Move to layer… and press Move…. A list shows what goes along — parts, own statblock, inventory and pieces, ticked when they lie in the same old layer — and where else each one is linked. Untick what should stay; Undo move takes the whole move back.

Set one article's visibility right in its row (Public, Table, Players, GM; ↺ follows the group again), or click a player to show or hide it for that player only. Tick several, or “all shown”, and set it for all at once. Articles in a layer you do not write get a rule of this campaign (see above). To move articles, tick them and use Move to layer…, or Edit › Layer on the article.
Your layers (“Make default” chooses where new articles go) and API tokens for scripts.

sections.heading: What stays here
text: Everything you deleted from your write layer stays here for 30 days, grouped by when it was deleted. Each group says until when it can come back.
Players see what they deleted themselves; the GM also sees what others deleted, as far as the GM may see those articles.

Restore brings one article back — with the parts that went with it (an inventory, a statblock instance) and its links to articles that are here. Restore all brings back the rest of a group. A restored article is linked from its row.

Empty trash deletes everything you see here for good: images then lose their file too, unless another image uses the same file, and the Workbench cannot undo it any more. After 30 days this happens on its own.
You reach this page from Account › Deleted articles, and from the message after deleting.
What changed on this site, newest first; filter by area. The dot in the header goes out once you have read it. The ? on each page shows the entries for that page.

sections.heading: Chapters
text: Everything the app explains, on one page: first steps, the help of every page, rules and options, workflows, the article types and the glossary. The list at the top jumps to a chapter.

sections.heading: Glossary
text: Search by term, alias, definition or translation; the letters jump, the buttons filter by sort. Click a term to open it beside the page, with how it affects play, examples and where it is used.
In any text, glossary terms are underlined with dots: hover or click for a preview, Ctrl/⌘+click to open the entry.

sections.heading: Turning it on
text: The rule builder is an experiment for game masters and admins. Turn it on in a campaign’s Rules & options › Experiments; the switch applies to your account only.

sections.heading: Building a rule
text: A rule is a chain of nodes: a trigger (a creature is hit, picks up an object …), conditions with a yes and a no exit, and outcomes such as offering a reaction. Add nodes with Trigger, Condition and Outcome; drag a node to move it.

Drag from a dot on a node’s right edge onto another node to connect them, or pick “Connect to” beside the canvas. Conditions compare numbers (distance, self.hp, self.reactionFree …), check whether a creature knows something by name, whether two roles are the same creature, or whether they stand on the same side (the party and its allies against everyone else).
An offered reaction can be a melee attack: then accepting it attacks the creature it is aimed at. Whether rules act in the turn plan is the campaign option Rules from graphs.

Every rule is a rule article, and Save writes into it: name, text, the options’ texts, its system and the nodes. New rule creates an article in your write layer; Open article shows it as a page. Add examples creates the sample rules that are missing. Rules the app runs on (those on Rules & options) cannot be deleted here.

sections.heading: Rules by engine
text: The list on the left groups the rules by system — the system articles, from reactions and spellcasting to inventory and crafting. Search by name or node text, or narrow it to one system, one trigger or active rules only. A rule with options lists them under its text.
Under its name a rule shows its text, and below it the text of the articles it is based on — the spell, feat or rule in its book; Edit text changes the rule’s own words.

“Builds on” names the glossary terms a rule rests on — from its trigger, the values its conditions read and its outcomes, and from its text; tap one to open it in the glossary. A dashed word has no glossary term yet.
On a phone, swipe on the empty canvas to scroll it; a node or dot takes the swipe for itself. − and + zoom, Fit shrinks the rule to the width of the screen.

sections.heading: Trying it
text: Try it holds made-up creatures. Pick an event, who acts and against whom, and Run: the page lists what fires and colours the path through the rule. Nothing is saved and nothing changes at the table.

Amount is the number of the event — damage taken, spell level — and conditions read it as amount. More values gives a creature further numbers such as maxHp=20 or slots1=2. Tap a result to open its rule with the path.

Shapes and stack sizes for the grid inventory, from groups instead of one by one. Left the groups, which come with the Grid mechanic of the rule system, right the items with the shape that applies and where it comes from: on the item, own shape, from a reference item, drawn by price (art objects) or from the group.

Pick a group to change its shape (rows like ##/## — # taken, . free), stack size, whether its items are carried at all, and its reference item: if that item has its own shape, it is the group’s shape. Every item of the group without its own follows the change.

Edit on an item sets what is local to it: its group, its reference item (a +1 Longsword takes the Longsword’s shape), an own shape or stack size, or No shape. “local” marks items with such a setting; Only local overrides lists just those, Clear local takes it back. A shape painted on the item itself still wins.

Writes to says which layer the changes go into — a default-shapes layer you write that is turned on in this campaign. Without one the page is read only; turn on the rule system Inventory on the campaign page.

without: The start only leads on: players to their campaign board, everyone else to the compendium.
without.login: Before signing in there is no header and no help button.
